## Definition

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

## Definition

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$. Let
the state dimension at time
$t$ be a positive integer $d_t$ for $0\le t\le T$, and the observation
dimension at time $t$ be a positive integer $p_t$ for $1\le t\le T$.
Choose deterministic matrices
$F_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_{t-1}}$ and
$H_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times d_t}$, a mean $m_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0}$, and
symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices, meaning $v^TPv\ge0$ for every
real vector $v$ of matching dimension,
$P_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0\times d_0}$,
$Q_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_t}$, and
$R_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times p_t}$. A **linear-Gaussian state-space model
with independent noises** is the general finite-horizon kernel model
([[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]) with initial law
$\mu_0=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$ and transition and observation kernels
$$K_t(x,\cdot)=N_{d_t}(F_t x,Q_t),\qquad G_t(x,\cdot)=N_{p_t}(H_t x,R_t).$$
All Gaussian laws use the convention of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]], which allows singular covariance matrices.

Its independent-noise representation consists of random vectors
$x_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T$ on a common probability space, with
$x_0\sim N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$, $q_t\sim N_{d_t}(0,Q_t)$,
$r_t\sim N_{p_t}(0,R_t)$, all mutually independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-random-elements]] (their generated sigma-algebras are
independent), and equations
$$x_t=F_t x_{t-1}+q_t,\qquad y_t=H_t x_t+r_t\qquad(1\le t\le T).$$
The local path-law theorem proves that every allowed parameter tuple has
such a finite representation, that its induced kernels are the displayed
$K_t,G_t$, and that its path law is the general kernel-product law.

This definition imposes the stated noise law and independence assumptions;
it does not establish their empirical adequacy. It supplies no filtering
algorithm, posterior recursion, or convergence claim. Any separate formula
that inverts an observed innovation covariance must assume that covariance is
positive definite at the point of inversion.

## Definition

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$. For
$0\le t\le T$, let
$(E_t,\mathcal E_t)$ be a standard-Borel state space; for $1\le t\le T$, let
$(F_t,\mathcal F_t)$ be a standard-Borel observation space
([[def-standard-borel-space]]), meaning a measurable space bimeasurably
isomorphic to a Polish space. A probability kernel has probability-measure
sections and measurable evaluations as in
[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Specify an initial probability
measure $\mu_0$ on $E_0$ (a measure of total mass one, as in
[[def-probability-measure]]), transition probability kernels $K_t$ from
$E_{t-1}$ to $E_t$, and observation probability kernels $G_t$ from $E_t$ to
$F_t$, for $1\le t\le T$.

The trajectory space, with the finite product sigma-algebra generated by
measurable coordinate rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]), is
$$\mathcal Z_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times F_T,$$
with $\mathcal Z_0=E_0$. Its finite-horizon law $P_T$ is the unique probability
law whose ordered iterated kernel integral is
$$\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{t=1}^T K_t(x_{t-1},dx_t)G_t(x_t,dy_t).$$
The product notation means successive integration in the displayed order; it
does not assert the existence of densities. Existence and uniqueness under AC
are proved in [[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]].
Every finite product trajectory space is standard Borel by
[[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]].

The initial and transition laws specify the state evolution, while each
$G_t$ specifies the observation law given the current state in this model.
State evolution by itself therefore does not specify a joint state-observation
law. No density or time-homogeneity assumption is imposed, and no strict
stationarity assumption (shift invariance of all finite-dimensional laws) is
required ([[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]]). This is a
single law, not a parameter-indexed family. The model contract records a
proposed law and makes no claim that it adequately describes an application
([[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]]).

## Definition

Let
$$\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). When the model is
parametric, write $\mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). A **scientific statistical model
contract** is an explicit record of the following fields for a specified
analysis.

1. **Observation space and record.** Give $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and say
   which values form one recorded data object. A response and each predictor
   used as a function of the data must be a specified measurable map from this
   space to a named measurable target. This is the map convention for a
   statistic in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]; it does not make a predictor
   causal or the response law correct.

2. **Scientific, sampling, assignment, and analysis units.** Name the
   biological or physical unit about which the scientific question is asked,
   the sample unit selected for observation when sampling occurs, the
   assignment unit receiving a randomized treatment when randomization occurs,
   and the analysis unit represented in each data record. These roles may
   differ. A technical replicate is a repeated reading or assay of the same
   specimen; a biological replicate is a distinct biological unit. Neither
   term asserts independence. State whether enrollment is a probability
   sample or a specified convenience/design cohort.

3. **Indices and time.** Give every unit, treatment, visit, and repeated
   measurement index, the object each index identifies, and the time origin.
   In particular, do not identify a participant index with a visit or assay
   index merely because all are written as rows in a data array.

4. **Quantity status.** Mark each model quantity as **fixed** (held
   nonrandom under the declared law), **random** (a measurable random element
   with its law specified, using [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]
   and [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]), **observed** (recorded
   in the data object), or **latent** (part of a fuller model state but not
   recorded). A latent quantity must separately be declared fixed or random.
   If inference conditions on a design value or event, name it and state the
   conditional law being used.

5. **Target and estimand.** Name the target population of units, settings,
   and time period, and distinguish it from the enrolled or observed sample.
   Specify the target as a function $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T$ when it is an
   estimand in the parametric model, as in
   [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]. The contract alone does not show
   that the target is identifiable. Identifiability means that equality of
   sampling laws forces equality of target values
   ([[def-identifiability-of-an-estimand]]).

6. **Observation mechanism.** State how a fuller scientific state becomes
   the recorded data. A deterministic mechanism is a specified measurable map
   $O:(\mathcal W,\mathcal G)\to(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. A stochastic
   mechanism is specified by $K:\mathcal W\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ such that,
   for each $w$, $A\mapsto K(w,A)$ is a probability measure and, for each
   $A\in\mathcal A$, $w\mapsto K(w,A)$ is measurable. These clauses define the
   mechanism supplied by the contract; they do not assert that a conditional
   version exists for an arbitrary joint law.

7. **Support and law.** State the sampling law $P_\theta$ on
   $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. For an asserted support set, give a measurable
   $S_\theta\subseteq\mathcal X$ with $P_\theta(S_\theta)=1$. If “support”
   instead means topological support, name the topology and the conditions
   under which that convention is being used. If densities are used, name the
   dominating measure and state whether their positive sets agree across
   parameter values. For a randomized design, also state its assignment law;
   if inference averages over assignments, give the resulting joint law.

8. **Conditioning convention.** Say whether inference uses the joint law,
   averaging over the declared randomization, or a specified conditional law
   given the realized design. A conditional law at an event of probability
   zero must be supplied as a specified version with its existence
   hypotheses; it is not defined by an ordinary probability ratio.

9. **Adequacy assumptions.** List each scientific adequacy assumption and
   classify it as **design-controlled** (imposed by protocol and checked
   against implementation records), **empirically assessable** (data or
   validation measurements can challenge it, without proving it true), or
   **substantively untestable** from the declared observed-data law (external
   domain evidence or additional assumptions are needed). Split an assumption
   that has different parts into separate entries and justify each label.

These are bookkeeping and interpretation requirements. They do not assert that
an empirical law equals a proposed model, that a design was implemented as
specified, that calibration is valid, or that any scientific or physical
application is adequate. No independence, exchangeability, missingness,
causal-identification, or common-support assumption follows from the indexing
or the classification labels. This definition uses no axiom of choice.

## Definition

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
(Measurable spaces and measurable sets). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

## Definition

Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$. For each integer $k$ with $0\le k\le T$, let $V_k$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space with an ordered basis $\Phi_k=(\phi_{k,1},\ldots,\phi_{k,m_k})$, where $m_k\ge1$. An ordered basis is a linearly independent spanning list. A coefficient vector $a_k=(a_{k,1},\ldots,a_{k,m_k})^T\in\mathbb R^{m_k}$ represents the trial field $u_k=\sum_{j=1}^{m_k}a_{k,j}\phi_{k,j}\in V_k$. This is a finite-dimensional representation; it does not assert that a fluid field in an untruncated model belongs to $V_k$.

For each $1\le k\le T$, choose a real linear observation map $L_k:V_k\to\mathbb R^{p_k}$, with $p_k\ge1$, and a real matrix $F_k\in\mathbb R^{m_k\times m_{k-1}}$ for the coefficient transition. The observation matrix $H_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k\times m_k}$ is defined by $[H_k]_{ij}=[L_k(\phi_{k,j})]_i$; hence $L_k(u_k)=H_ka_k$. A symmetric matrix $C$ is positive semidefinite, written $C\succeq0$, when $v^TCv\ge0$ for every vector $v$ of matching dimension, and is positive definite, written $C\succ0$, when this inequality is strict for every nonzero $v$.

For stochastic assimilation, assume the Axiom of Choice (AC), meaning every family of nonempty sets has a choice function, for the Gaussian-law construction. Choose an instance of the finite linear-Gaussian state-space model with independent noises: $a_0\sim N_{m_0}(\mu_0,P_0)$, $q_k\sim N_{m_k}(0,Q_k)$, and $r_k\sim N_{p_k}(0,R_k)$ are mutually independent, with $P_0,Q_k,R_k\succeq0$, and
$$a_k=F_ka_{k-1}+q_k,\qquad y_k=H_ka_k+r_k.$$
Here $N_d(\mu,C)$ denotes the $d$-dimensional Gaussian law with mean $\mu$ and symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance $C$, including singular $C$. For a Kalman-filter run, write $m^a_{k-1}$ and $P^a_{k-1}$ for its previous analysis mean and covariance, and define its forecast mean and covariance, innovation, and innovation covariance by
$$m^f_k=F_km^a_{k-1},\qquad P^f_k=F_kP^a_{k-1}F_k^T+Q_k,\qquad d_k=y_k-H_km^f_k,\qquad S_k=H_kP^f_kH_k^T+R_k.$$
The admissible filter inputs are those for which each innovation covariance to be solved is positive definite. The gain is the solution $K_k=P^f_kH_k^TS_k^{-1}$, computed by the supplied Cholesky solves, and the analysis outputs are $m^a_k=m^f_k+K_kd_k$ and $P^a_k=P^f_k-K_kS_kK_k^T$. The formula describes the exact target of the supplied recursion; it is not an instruction to form a matrix inverse numerically.

For a one-step perturbed-observation ensemble Kalman update, choose dimensions $m,p\ge1$, a linear observation matrix $H\in\mathbb R^{p\times m}$, a datum $y\in\mathbb R^p$, an ensemble size $N\ge2$, and a positive-definite observation covariance $\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$. Given forecast coefficients $\hat a^1,\ldots,\hat a^N\in\mathbb R^m$, take perturbations $\eta^i\sim N_p(0,\Gamma)$ independent across members and independent of the forecast ensemble. Define $\bar a=N^{-1}\sum_i\hat a^i$ and the divisor-$N$ covariance $C_N=N^{-1}\sum_i(\hat a^i-\bar a)(\hat a^i-\bar a)^T$. The gain and perturbed-data update are $K_N=C_NH^T(HC_NH^T+\Gamma)^{-1}$ and $a^{a,i}=\hat a^i+K_N(y+\eta^i-H\hat a^i)$. Since $C_N\succeq0$, $HC_NH^T+\Gamma\succ0$. This is the specified finite-ensemble procedure; the definition alone gives no finite-ensemble posterior-exactness claim.

In a single-window finite inverse view, a real matrix $G\in\mathbb R^{p\times m}$ maps coefficients $a\in\mathbb R^m$ to predicted observations $Ga$. A datum has the form $y=Ga+e$, where $e\in\mathbb R^p$ is its realized error and a symmetric positive-definite matrix $R\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ is the declared error covariance and weighting matrix. This deterministic inverse interface does not assume a probability distribution for the realized vector $e$.

Choosing a finite trial space, a linearization, or process-noise covariances is part of adopting the finite model. These choices do not show that a nonlinear fluid equation or an actual sensor is described exactly by that model.

## Statement

Let $E$ be a nonzero linear subspace of the finite coefficient space $\mathbb R^m$, let $G:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^p$ be the declared linear observation map, and let $R\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric positive definite. Let $R^{1/2}$ be the unique symmetric positive-semidefinite square root of $R$ and set $W=(R^{1/2})^{-1}$, so $W^TW=R^{-1}$. The whitened map is $A=W(G|_E):E\to\mathbb R^p$, and define its smallest gain by $\sigma_{\min}(A)=\inf\{\|Av\|_2:v\in E,\ \|v\|_2=1\}$; the singular-value decomposition shows this infimum is the smallest singular value and is attained. Identifiability on $E$ means injectivity of $G|_E$. It holds exactly when $\sigma_{\min}(A)>0$. If it holds, then for every true $a\in E$, every realized error $e\in\mathbb R^p$, and datum $y=Ga+e$, the unique weighted least-squares estimate $\hat a=\arg\min_{b\in E}\|W(y-Gb)\|_2$ satisfies
$$\|\hat a-a\|_2\le\frac{\|We\|_2}{\sigma_{\min}(A)}.$$
If $\sigma_{\min}(A)=0$, a nonzero vector in $E\cap\ker G$ makes distinct coefficients observationally indistinguishable. The estimate is pointwise in the realized error; it is not a confidence or probability statement. If a pressure representation includes an additive-constant coefficient direction in $\ker G$, that direction must be fixed or quotiented out to obtain identifiable coefficients. This finite-dimensional result is not a general coefficient-identifiability theorem for a partial differential equation.

[F2] Every linear map between finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces has orthonormal domain and codomain bases in which it acts by its nonnegative singular values and is zero on the remaining domain basis vectors. [[thm-singular-value-decomposition]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Since $R\succ0$, it is positive semidefinite, so [F1] gives a symmetric positive-semidefinite $S$ with $S^2=R$. If $Sv=0$, then $Rv=S^2v=0$, and positive definiteness of $R$ forces $v=0$; hence $S$ is invertible. Therefore $W=S^{-1}$ is symmetric positive definite and $W^TW=S^{-2}=R^{-1}$. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

1.2 Apply [F2] to $A$ on the nonzero finite-dimensional inner-product space $E$: for an orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ of $E$, the SVD gives $r\le\min(d,p)$ positive singular values $s_1,\ldots,s_r$, an orthonormal list $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ in $\mathbb R^p$, $Ae_i=s_if_i$ for $i\le r$, and $Ae_i=0$ for $i>r$. For $v=\sum_i c_ie_i$ with $\|v\|_2=1$, $\|Av\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^r s_i^2c_i^2$. Thus the infimum in the Statement is zero when $r<d$ and is $\min_i s_i$ when $r=d$; it is positive exactly when $A$ is injective. If $r<d$, any $e_j$ with $j>r$ is a nonzero kernel vector. [F2, given, algebra]

2.1 The operator $W$ is invertible by step 1.1, so for every $v\in E$, $Av=0$ if and only if $WGv=0$, which holds if and only if $Gv=0$. Thus $A$ is injective exactly when $G|_E$ is injective, and in the noninjective case a nonzero $v\in E\cap\ker G$ gives $G(a+v)=Ga$ for every $a\in E$. [A1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Suppose $\sigma_{\min}(A)>0$. Step 1.2 then has $r=d\le p$, so the $d$ vectors $f_1,\ldots,f_d$ form an orthonormal list that extends to an orthonormal basis $f_1,\ldots,f_p$ of $\mathbb R^p$ by [F2]. Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC), meaning every family of nonempty sets has a choice function, for the Gaussian-law construction. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, positive integers $m_k$ for $0\le k\le T$ and $p_k$ for $1\le k\le T$, matrices $F_k\in\mathbb R^{m_k\times m_{k-1}}$ and $H_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k\times m_k}$ for $1\le k\le T$, and a finite linear-Gaussian coefficient model
$$a_k=F_ka_{k-1}+q_k,\qquad y_k=H_ka_k+r_k,$$
where $\mu_0\in\mathbb R^{m_0}$, $a_0\sim N_{m_0}(\mu_0,P_0)$, $q_k\sim N_{m_k}(0,Q_k)$, and $r_k\sim N_{p_k}(0,R_k)$ are mutually independent, $P_0,Q_k$ are positive semidefinite, and $R_k$ is positive definite. Fix arbitrary observation data $y_{1:T}$. For each ensemble size $N\ge2$, draw the initial members $a_{N,i}^{a,0}$ independently from $N_{m_0}(\mu_0,P_0)$. At each $k$, draw process perturbations $q_{N,i}^k\sim N_{m_k}(0,Q_k)$ and observation perturbations $\eta_{N,i}^k\sim N_{p_k}(0,R_k)$, with all these perturbations mutually independent across members and times and independent of the initial ensemble, and set $a_{N,i}^{f,k}=F_ka_{N,i}^{a,k-1}+q_{N,i}^k$. Define $\bar a_N^{f,k}=N^{-1}\sum_i a_{N,i}^{f,k}$ and the divisor-$N$ covariance $C_N^{f,k}=N^{-1}\sum_i(a_{N,i}^{f,k}-\bar a_N^{f,k})(a_{N,i}^{f,k}-\bar a_N^{f,k})^T$. The common gain and perturbed-observation update are
$$K_N^k=C_N^{f,k}H_k^T(H_kC_N^{f,k}H_k^T+R_k)^{-1},\qquad a_{N,i}^{a,k}=a_{N,i}^{f,k}+K_N^k(y_k+\eta_{N,i}^k-H_ka_{N,i}^{f,k}).$$
Since $C_N^{f,k}$ is positive semidefinite and $R_k$ is positive definite, this inverse exists. Define the analysis empirical mean and covariance by $\bar a_N^{a,k}=N^{-1}\sum_i a_{N,i}^{a,k}$ and $C_N^{a,k}=N^{-1}\sum_i(a_{N,i}^{a,k}-\bar a_N^{a,k})(a_{N,i}^{a,k}-\bar a_N^{a,k})^T$. Let $m_{k|k}$ and $P_{k|k}$ be the mean and covariance produced by the exact Kalman recursion in the preceding filtering proposition, which defines an everywhere-defined Gaussian filtering law at every fixed history $y_{1:k}$. At each fixed $k\le T$, $\bar a_N^{a,k}$ and $C_N^{a,k}$ converge in probability to $m_{k|k}$ and $P_{k|k}$ as $N\to\infty$; moreover, for each fixed bounded Lipschitz function $\varphi:\mathbb R^{m_k}\to\mathbb R$, $N^{-1}\sum_i\varphi(a_{N,i}^{a,k})$ converges in probability to its integral under that filtering law. Here bounded Lipschitz means $\sup_x|\varphi(x)|<\infty$ and $|\varphi(x)-\varphi(x')|\le L\|x-x'\|_2$ for some finite $L$ and all $x,x'$. Convergence in probability means that for every $\epsilon>0$, the probability that the error exceeds $\epsilon$ tends to zero; use Euclidean norm for vectors, Frobenius norm for matrices, and absolute value for scalars. All probabilities refer to the ensemble sampling just described. The horizon is fixed as $N$ grows, with no uniform-in-time conclusion. At finite $N$, the common sample-covariance gain couples the update, and the theorem does not assert independent posterior samples or an exact posterior law for the ensemble. It covers the stated linear maps and perturbed-observation formula only. Covariance localization here means replacing the sample covariance by its entrywise product with a prescribed taper matrix; covariance inflation means rescaling the ensemble anomalies by a factor greater than one or adding a prescribed positive-semidefinite covariance; a transport update means applying a selected map to ensemble members instead of the displayed perturbed-observation formula. These modified procedures and nonlinear state or observation maps require their own statements and proofs. The claim is conditional on the chosen finite model; it is not a conclusion that a nonlinear fluid equation or an actual flow is described by it.

## Postulate

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $E$ be a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space. Fix an orientation-preserving affine isometry $x:E\to\mathbb R^3$ as the Cartesian inertial chart on Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$, with absolute time $t$ in seconds and spatial position in metres. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded Lebesgue-measurable observation region with volume $0<|D|<\infty$, and let $\mathcal H=L^2(D;\mathbb R^3)$ be the space of almost-everywhere equivalence classes of square-integrable vector fields, with norm $\|v\|_{\mathcal H}=(\int_D|v(x)|^2\,d^3x)^{1/2}$. Write $\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ for the sigma-algebra generated by the norm-open sets. A velocity field has units m s$^{-1}$.

Choose an integer observation horizon $T\ge0$ and times $t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_T$ in $I$, where observations are taken at $t_1,\ldots,t_T$. For each $0\le k\le T$, let $m_k\ge1$ and choose dimensionless modal fields $\phi_{k,1},\ldots,\phi_{k,m_k}\in\mathcal H$. Define the modal map $\Phi_k:\mathbb R^{m_k}\to\mathcal H$ by $\Phi_k(a)=\sum_{j=1}^{m_k}a_j\phi_{k,j}$. The coefficient vector $a_k\in\mathbb R^{m_k}$ has units m s$^{-1}$, with initial mean $\mu_0$ in m s$^{-1}$, and its represented velocity field is $U_k=\Phi_k(a_k)$. This finite-dimensional representation is an adopted approximation for the selected observation times; it does not assert that an untruncated fluid field lies in one of these finite-dimensional spaces.

For each $1\le k\le T$, choose $p_k\ge1$ sensor weights $\psi_{k,1},\ldots,\psi_{k,p_k}\in\mathcal H$, with units m$^{-3}$. The ideal sensor on a field $v\in\mathcal H$ is the weighted spatial average $S_{\psi_{k,i}}(v)=\int_D v(x)\cdot\psi_{k,i}(x)\,d^3x$; it is not a point evaluation. Define $L_k:\operatorname{span}\{\phi_{k,1},\ldots,\phi_{k,m_k}\}\to\mathbb R^{p_k}$ by $(L_kv)_i=S_{\psi_{k,i}}(v)$ and define the dimensionless observation matrix by $[H_k]_{ij}=(L_k\phi_{k,j})_i$. Thus $L_k(U_k)=H_ka_k$, and each datum and observation-noise component has units m s$^{-1}$.

On a common probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, adopt the finite linear-Gaussian coefficient model
$$a_0\sim N_{m_0}(\mu_0,P_0),\qquad a_k=F_ka_{k-1}+q_k,\qquad y_k=H_ka_k+r_k\quad(1\le k\le T),$$

The vectors $a_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T$ are mutually independent. Here $N_d(\mu,C)$ denotes the $d$-dimensional Gaussian law with mean $\mu$ and covariance $C$, including singular covariance. A symmetric matrix $C$ is positive semidefinite, written $C\succeq0$, if $z^TCz\ge0$ for every vector $z$ of the matching dimension. The covariance matrices $P_0,Q_k,R_k$ have this property, with entries carrying the corresponding squared units. Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC), meaning every family of nonempty sets has a choice function, for the Gaussian-law construction. The finite-dimensional Gaussian laws and their common probability-space realization use this assumption. For each $k$, define the field law by $\mu_k(B)=\mathbb P(U_k\in B)$ for $B\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$; finite modal fields with finite-second-moment coefficients have finite-second-moment laws.

These linearity, Gaussianity, independence, covariance, finite-mode, and ideal-sensor conditions are adopted physical-model assumptions for this selected regime. The sensor weights and covariance matrices are model inputs; no calibration procedure is asserted. These conditions report no measurements and do not assert that an actual flow, observation system, or noise source satisfies them. $$m_{k|k-1}=F_km_{k-1|k-1},\qquad P_{k|k-1}=F_kP_{k-1|k-1}F_k^T+Q_k,$$
$$v_k=y_k-H_km_{k|k-1},\qquad S_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k.$$
Here $\mu_0\in\mathbb R^{m_0}$, $F_k\in\mathbb R^{m_k\times m_{k-1}}$, $H_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k\times m_k}$, $P_0\in\mathbb R^{m_0\times m_0}$, $Q_k\in\mathbb R^{m_k\times m_k}$, and $R_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k\times p_k}$. Assume every $S_k$ to be inverted is positive definite, meaning $z^TS_kz>0$ for every nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$. Set
$$K_k=P_{k|k-1}H_k^TS_k^{-1},\qquad m_{k|k}=m_{k|k-1}+K_kv_k,\qquad P_{k|k}=P_{k|k-1}-K_kS_kK_k^T.$$
Write $y_{1:k}=(y_1,\ldots,y_k)$, let $y_{1:0}$ be the singleton empty history, and let $\nu_k$ be the probability law of $y_{1:k}$. For every $0\le k\le T$, the Gaussian kernel $\pi_k(y_{1:k},\cdot)=N_{m_k}(m_{k|k},P_{k|k})$ is a probability kernel from histories to coefficient-state laws and satisfies the regular-conditional-law identities: for every Borel state set $A\subseteq\mathbb R^{m_k}$ and Borel history set $B\subseteq\prod_{j=1}^k\mathbb R^{p_j}$, $\mathbb P(a_k\in A,\ y_{1:k}\in B)=\int_B\pi_k(y,A)\,\nu_k(dy)$. For $k=0$, the history space is a singleton and $\pi_0=N_{m_0}(\mu_0,P_0)$. If $U_k=\Phi_k(a_k)$ is the represented velocity field, its regular conditional law is the pushforward kernel
$$\rho_k(y_{1:k},C)=\pi_k(y_{1:k},\Phi_k^{-1}(C))\qquad(C\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)).$$
Both kernels are defined at every observation history, including histories with probability zero; this selects a version and asserts no pointwise uniqueness there. The result is exact for the declared finite model and does not assert that an untruncated or nonlinear fluid flow, an actual sensor, or actual noise follows that model.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the finite-horizon coefficient and observation equations; mutually independent Gaussian initial, process, and observation vectors with positive-semidefinite covariances; positive-definite innovation covariances; finite modal maps; and weighted spatial sensors as in the Statement.

[A1] AC is the axiom that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function; it is assumed for the Gaussian-law construction. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The physical framework uses absolute time and an adapted Cartesian inertial chart on Newtonian spacetime; its Eulerian velocity has units m s$^{-1}$. [[def-fd-quantity-and-frame-conventions]]

[F2] The sensor is the weighted spatial integral $S_\psi(v)=\int_Dv\cdot\psi\,d^3x$ on almost-everywhere classes in $\mathcal H=L^2(D;\mathbb R^3)$; it is not a point evaluation. [[def-fd-random-velocity-sensor-law]]

[F3] Each sensor pairing is finite, representative-independent, linear, and bounded on $\mathcal H$. [[lem-fd-sensor-pairing-is-well-defined]]

[F4] Under AC, if a measurable coefficient vector has finite second moment, the finite modal lemma gives a strongly measurable field and a finite-second-moment pushforward law; its Statement does not claim modal-map continuity. [[lem-fd-finite-modal-field-has-finite-second-moment]]

[F5] The physical postulate adopts the finite-dimensional coefficient state equation, weighted sensor observation equation, and independent Gaussian noise assumptions; it does not assert empirical adequacy. [[post-fd-fluid-observation-and-noise]]

[F6] The finite linear-Gaussian state-space convention has $a_k=F_ka_{k-1}+q_k$ and $y_k=H_ka_k+r_k$, with mutually independent Gaussian vectors and positive-semidefinite covariances, including singular ones. [[def-fd-fluid-coefficient-observation-model]]

[F7] Under AC and positive-definite solved innovations, the declared finite coefficient model has the stated exact Gaussian conditional law at every observation history, including singular state and noise covariances. [[prop-fd-linear-fluid-filter-interface]]

[F8] A filtering kernel is an everywhere-defined probability kernel whose composition with the observation history is a regular conditional distribution of the state; it satisfies the conditional event identities on every Borel history set. [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]

[F9] The finite coefficient observation matrix is defined by $[H_k]_{ij}=[L_k(\phi_{k,j})]_i$, so the field observation equals $H_ka_k$. [[def-fd-fluid-coefficient-observation-model]]

[F10] The space $\mathcal H=L^2(D;\mathbb R^3)$ has its stated norm, which satisfies the norm triangle inequality. [[def-fd-random-velocity-sensor-law]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and notation of the Statement.

1.1 In the fixed Cartesian inertial chart of [F1], for each $k$ and coefficient vector $a$, the weighted sensor maps in [F2] and postulate [F5] use finite linearity of the pairings [F3] to give
$$(L_k(\Phi_k(a)))_i=S_{\psi_{k,i}}\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^{m_k}a_j\phi_{k,j}\right)=\sum_{j=1}^{m_k}a_jS_{\psi_{k,i}}(\phi_{k,j})=\sum_{j=1}^{m_k}[H_k]_{ij}a_j.$$
All terms are defined because $\phi_{k,j},\psi_{k,i}\in\mathcal H$ and [F3] makes each pairing finite. By the matrix definition in [F9], this is exactly the finite coefficient observation equation. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F9, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F5] and [F6], the coefficient equations, dimensions, mutual independence, and covariance conventions match the finite linear-Gaussian interface. Step 1.1 identifies its matrix observation map with the specified physical sensor. The explicit AC assumption [A1] and positive-definite $S_k$ hypotheses are exactly the remaining assumptions of [F7]. Thus every hypothesis of the exact coefficient filtering result [F7] holds. [A1, F5, F6, F7, given, step 1.1]

3.1 For each $k$, put $C_k=\sum_{j=1}^{m_k}\|\phi_{k,j}\|_{\mathcal H}$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^{m_k}$, the norm triangle inequality [F10] gives
$$\|\Phi_k(a)-\Phi_k(b)\|_{\mathcal H}\le\sum_{j=1}^{m_k}|a_j-b_j|\|\phi_{k,j}\|_{\mathcal H}\le C_k|a-b|,$$
because each coordinate satisfies $|a_j-b_j|\le|a-b|$. Thus $\Phi_k$ is continuous. This estimate is derived here; the finite-second-moment lemma [F4] does not assert continuity. [F10, given, algebra]

4.1 Apply [F7] to obtain the coefficient regular conditional kernel $\pi_k$ at every history. By step 3.1, $\Phi_k^{-1}(C)$ is Borel for every $C\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$. For each history $y$, $C\mapsto\pi_k(y,\Phi_k^{-1}(C))$ is a probability measure, and for each Borel $C$ its value is measurable in $y$ by the kernel property; hence $\rho_k$ is a probability kernel. For any Borel observation-history set $B$, the defining conditional-law identity in [F8] therefore gives
$$\mathbb P(U_k\in C,\ y_{1:k}\in B)=\mathbb P(a_k\in\Phi_k^{-1}(C),\ y_{1:k}\in B)=\int_B\pi_k(y,\Phi_k^{-1}(C))\,\nu_k(dy).$$
The last integrand is $\rho_k(y,C)$, so the conditional event identity holds for $U_k$ and $\rho_k$ is its regular conditional law by [F8]. Because $\pi_k$ is defined at every history, so is its pushforward $\rho_k$, including on null histories. [F4, F7, F8, step 2.1, step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎
